In requests/utils.py, `get_environ_proxies(url, no_proxy=None)` (line 816) calls `should_bypass_proxies(url, no_proxy=no_proxy)`. If that returns True, it returns `{}`. Otherwise it returns `getproxies()`, which is the proxy mapping taken from the environment (http_proxy, https_proxy, all_proxy and so on).

In `should_bypass_proxies`, an explicit `no_proxy` argument takes precedence over the `no_proxy` environment variable. The code saves `no_proxy_arg = no_proxy`. It reads `get_proxy("no_proxy")` from the environment only when the argument is None. The bypass list is then matched against the URL hostname: IPv4 addresses are matched by CIDR or exact IP, and hostnames by suffix, with or without the port. The `set_environ("no_proxy", no_proxy_arg)` block also makes the platform's `proxy_bypass` use the same override.

A non-empty dict therefore means the URL did not match the caller-supplied no_proxy list, so no bypass applies and the environment proxies are used. An empty dict means the URL is exempt from proxying and the request goes direct. The environment's own no_proxy value is ignored whenever the keyword is given.

The test `test_not_bypass_no_proxy_keyword` in requests/tests/test_utils.py (lines 267-272) shows this. It sets `http_proxy`, passes `no_proxy="192.168.1.1,requests.com"`, and uses URLs that are not in that list. It asserts `get_environ_proxies(url, no_proxy=no_proxy) != {}`, which confirms the proxies are still applied. The companion test `test_bypass_no_proxy_keyword` (line 253) asserts `== {}` for URLs that do match the list.

The two are only loosely related. They sit in the same module, sqlfluff/src/sqlfluff/cli/formatters.py, but the header function does not use the formatter class or its stream.

`format_linting_result_header()` (line 62) is a standalone module-level function. It creates a `StringIO` buffer, writes "==== readout ====\n" into it, and returns `text_buffer.getvalue()`. The buffer is only a temporary in-memory place to build the string. The function returns a plain `str` and does not write to any output stream. `OutputStreamFormatter(FormatterInterface)` (line 69) is the class that manages formatted output streams. Its constructor takes an `OutputStream` and stores it as `_output_stream`. It also takes `verbosity`, `filter_empty`, `output_line_length`, `nocolor` and `show_lint_violations`. Its public methods format objects such as violations, configs and parse trees. The class's `_dispatch(s)` method then writes the text to the stream with `self._output_stream.write(s)`, skipping empty messages when `filter_empty` is set. Several of its helpers, such as `_format_config`, also build text in a `StringIO` buffer and return the string. That is the same pattern the header function uses.

In short, `StringIO` is the shared way to build strings in both places. The header function only builds and returns a string and is output-agnostic. The class formats text and sends it to the `OutputStream` through `_dispatch`, which is where destination, verbosity and filtering are handled.

test_pragmas (TestContentEncodingDetection, requests/tests/test_utils.py) is parametrized over four declaration styles: HTML5 `<meta charset="UTF-8">`, HTML4 pragma `<meta http-equiv="Content-type" content="text/html;charset=UTF-8">`, the same with `/>` (XHTML 1.x as text/html), and the XML prolog `<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>` (XHTML as XML). For each it calls get_encodings_from_content(content) and asserts exactly one encoding is returned (len == 1, no duplicates from overlapping regexes) and that it equals the bare string "UTF-8" — quotes, "text/html;" prefix and closing ">" or "/>" are stripped, and the name is returned as written. get_encodings_from_content (requests/src/requests/utils.py:479) concatenates results from three regexes: charset_re (`<meta.*?charset=["']*(.+?)["'>]`, case-insensitive), pragma_re (`<meta.*?content=["']*;?charset=(.+?)["'>]`) and xml_re (`^<\?xml.*?encoding=["']*(.+?)["'>]`, anchored at start). Only one regex matches each sample (charset_re matches both http-equiv forms; pragma_re needs charset= right after content=), hence a single result. It also emits a DeprecationWarning. Sibling tests: test_none (empty -> no encodings) and test_precedence (order HTML5, HTML4, XML). Note it parses content, not HTTP headers (that is get_encoding_from_headers).

The class doesn't use a named architectural pattern such as a mediator, dependency injection or an interface. It relies on plain Python import mechanics, and the "cycle" is only a test fixture for autodoc. The fixture is the package `sphinx/tests/roots/test-ext-autodoc/circular_import/`, and I read all four of its files.

- `circular_import/a.py` is only `X = 42`.
- `circular_import/b.py` is a type-only import. It contains `import typing` and then `if typing.TYPE_CHECKING: from circular_import import SomeClass`. That import is never executed at runtime, so `b` has no runtime dependency on the package.
- `circular_import/c.py` defines `SomeClass`. It uses module-object imports instead of `from … import` names: `import circular_import.a` and `import circular_import.b`. The class body then does `X = circular_import.a.X`.
- `circular_import/__init__.py` runs `from circular_import.c import SomeClass`, which is what pulls `c` in at package import time.

Because `c.py` imports the modules (`import circular_import.a`) and resolves the attribute only when the class body runs, the import of `c` never needs a name that isn't defined yet. `b.py` avoids a real cycle by importing `SomeClass` only under `typing.TYPE_CHECKING`.

So the technique is a combination of two things:
1. Deferred or qualified module-attribute access (`import pkg.mod` rather than `from pkg import name`).
2. A `TYPE_CHECKING`-guarded import that exists only for static typing.

Which cycle this fixture is meant to test was my inference from the file contents. I did not trace how the autodoc tests use it.

The wrappers are `FunctionalContext` and `Segments`, both in `sqlfluff.utils.functional`. They sit between rule LT09 (`Rule_LT09`, name `layout.select_targets`, in `sqlfluff/src/sqlfluff/rules/layout/LT09.py`) and the raw parse tree. This answer is based on the first 130 lines of LT09.py plus the ranked excerpts. I did not open the `sqlfluff.utils.functional` source, so the tuple-based nature of `Segments` and the details of `sp` come from the question and general knowledge, not from code I read.

**How LT09 uses them**
- `FunctionalContext(context).segment` wraps the `select_clause` segment from the `RuleContext` in a `Segments` object. `Segments` is a tuple-based collection of `BaseSegment`s with query methods.
- `_eval` calls `select_clause.children(sp.is_type("select_clause_element")).children(sp.is_type("wildcard_expression"))`. This chain finds wildcard targets without LT09 walking the tree itself.
- `_get_indexes` is a static method that builds a `SelectTargetsInfo` NamedTuple. It calls `children()` on the wrapped segment, then `select(sp.is_type(...))`, `select(sp.is_keyword("select"))` and `select(sp.is_type("newline"))`. It uses `find()` for indexes and `get()` for the first match. It also calls `select(..., start_seg=..., stop_seg=..., loop_while=sp.or_(...))` to detect a comment between `SELECT` and the first newline.
- Later in the rule, around line 167, the code uses `Segments(select_target).raw_segments.first(sp.is_code()).get()` to find the first code token of a select target.
- `sp` (segment predicates) supplies the predicates: `is_type`, `is_keyword`, `is_code`, `is_meta`, `or_`.

**Architectural role**
- **Query layer:** Rules express "find the select keyword, newlines, targets and comments" as declarative, chainable queries (`children`, `select`, `find`, `first`, `get`, `raw_segments`). They do not hand-write recursion over `BaseSegment.segments` or index into it.
- **Decoupling:** LT09 depends on the functional API and on segment type names, not on how `BaseSegment` stores its children. The tree internals can change without touching the rule.
- **Safe results:** Collections are tuple-like, so they are immutable and falsy when empty. That is why the rule can write `if newlines`, `if comment_after_select` and `bool(wildcards)` without None checks.
- **Rule logic separated from fixes:** The rule gathers positions into `SelectTargetsInfo`. The `_eval_single_select_target_element` and `_eval_multiple_select_target_elements` branches then decide the lint result and `LintFix`es from that summary.
- **Reuse:** The same wrappers are used in other rules such as AL03 and CV11. `functional.rst` describes them as helpers for rules that navigate or search the parse tree.

InvalidSchema (requests/src/requests/exceptions.py:103) is declared as `class InvalidSchema(RequestException, ValueError)`, with docstring "The URL scheme provided is either invalid or unsupported." The two parents have different roles:

- RequestException (itself a subclass of IOError, line 12) is the library's own base class. It marks the failure as a Requests-level error that happened while handling a request. Its __init__ takes optional `request` and `response` kwargs and stores them as attributes. Code that does `except requests.RequestException` therefore catches every Requests error, including bad schemas. This is the "ambiguous exception while handling your request" category, and it is I/O-flavoured.
- ValueError is the built-in for an argument that has the right type but an unacceptable value. Here the URL string is malformed or its scheme is unusable. It keeps backward compatibility, because HISTORY.md:1645 notes "ValueError for invalid schema URLs". Callers who wrote `except ValueError` still catch it. docs/api.rst:222-225 records that exceptions were reorganised under RequestException.

MissingSchema (line 99) uses the same pair of parents. The exception is raised in two places:

- adapters.py:63, with "Missing dependencies for SOCKS support."

Because of the dual inheritance, one exception can be caught either as a Requests failure (RequestException/IOError) or as a bad-value error (ValueError).

The mechanism is in `PyClasslike.get_index_text(self, modname, name_cls)` in sphinx/sphinx/domains/python/__init__.py. `PyClasslike` is the directive class for `class` and `exception`. It checks `self.objtype`, which is set from the directive name.

- If `objtype == 'class'` and there is no `modname`, it returns `_('%s (built-in class)') % name_cls[0]`.
- If `objtype == 'class'` and there is a `modname`, it returns `_('%s (class in %s)') % (name_cls[0], modname)`.
- If `objtype == 'exception'`, it returns just `name_cls[0]`, the bare name with no suffix.
- For any other objtype, it returns `''`, so no index entry is made.

Translation works through `_()`, which is Sphinx's gettext translation function. The format strings `'%s (built-in class)'` and `'%s (class in %s)'` are the message IDs. The `objtype` branch picks which message ID is looked up, and `_()` returns the localized template, which is then filled in with `%`. So the conditional decides which entry is produced, and translation decides how that entry is worded in the target language. Class and exception entries therefore differ in meaning as well as in text.

The caller is `PyObject.add_target_and_index` in sphinx/sphinx/domains/python/_object.py, near line 433. Unless the `no-index-entry` option is set, it calls `self.get_index_text(mod_name, name_cls)`. If the result is non-empty, it appends `('single', index_text, node_id, '', None)` to `self.indexnode['entries']`. Because the `else` branch returns `''`, the caller skips the entry.

The `StatementSegment` (type "statement", `dialect_ansi.py:4121`) has no custom tie-break code of its own. Its `match_grammar` is a `OneOf(...)` over `Ref`s to every statement type (`SelectableGrammar`, `MergeStatementSegment`, `InsertStatementSegment`, and so on). Dialect subclasses such as `StatementSegment(ansi.StatementSegment)` in tsql, postgres and others extend that list. `OneOf` (`core/parser/grammar/anyof.py:250`, a subclass of `AnyNumberOf`) is documented as: "If it matches multiple, it returns the longest, and if any are the same length it returns the first (unless we explicitly just match first)". It resolves ambiguity by calling `longest_match()` in `core/parser/match_algorithms.py:140`. I read `longest_match`, the `StatementSegment` definition and the `OneOf` docstring. I did not read `AnyNumberOf`'s code, so I did not confirm there that it calls `longest_match`. I did not read `MatchResult.is_better_than` either.

How `longest_match(segments, matchers, idx, parse_context)` works:
1. If there are no matchers or `idx` is at the end, it returns an empty match.
2. `prune_options()` first discards options that cannot start at this token, using each option's simple representation. This is a performance step.
3. It then tries each remaining matcher in order, in the order listed in the grammar. Each result goes through the parse cache (`check_parse_cache` / `put_parse_cache`), keyed on the first segment's raw text, position, type and `max_idx`.
4. If a match consumes everything up to `max_idx` (`res_match.matched_slice.stop == max_idx`), it returns that match immediately. This is a total match and has top priority.
5. Otherwise it keeps a running `best_match` and `best_matcher`. A candidate replaces them only if `res_match.is_better_than(best_match)`. The stated priority is:
   - the first total match, meaning all segments are matched or a valid terminator follows;
   - the longest clean match;
   - the longest unclean match;
   - an empty match.
   A tie on length goes to the earlier matcher in the list, because a later match must be strictly better to replace the current best.
6. Early exit: after a new best match, if it came from the last option, or if the next code segment after it is the end of input or matches one of `parse_context.terminators`, it sets `terminated` and stops. The first terminated match therefore wins, and later matchers are never tried.
7. It returns `(best_match, best_matcher)`.

CSVTable (sphinx/directives/patches.py, subclass of docutils tables.CSVTable, registered for 'csv-table' in setup()). Its run() uses the build environment (self.state.document.settings.env) to resolve paths: if the :file: option starts with '/' (SEP/os.sep) and the absolute path doesn't really exist on disk, it computes abspath = env.srcdir / file[1:], gets doc_dir = env.doc2path(env.current_document.docname).parent, and rewrites self.options['file'] = relpath(abspath, doc_dir), i.e. a path relative to the current document. Then it calls super().run(), so docutils' CSVTable reads the file and (via docutils' own dependency recording) tracks it. If the absolute path exists on the filesystem, it logs a warning (location=(env.current_document.docname, self.lineno)) that absolute paths are now treated as relative to the source dir. Note: there is no explicit env.note_dependency call here; the mechanism is env.srcdir + env.doc2path + relpath rewriting, with dependency tracking left to docutils' super().run().

- Direct subclasses of RequestException:

  - HTTPError
  - ConnectionError
  - Timeout
  - URLRequired
  - TooManyRedirects
  - ChunkedEncodingError
  - RetryError
  - UnrewindableBodyError

In sqlfluff's Exasol dialect, `RejectClauseSegment(BaseSegment)` (type "reject_clause", the REJECT clause of IMPORT/EXPORT statements) sets its `match_grammar` class attribute to a `Sequence` (the ordered-element grammar) imported from `sqlfluff.core.parser`. The Sequence is `Sequence("REJECT", "LIMIT", OneOf(Ref("NumericLiteralSegment"), "UNLIMITED"), Ref.keyword("ERRORS", optional=True))`. Sequence matches its elements strictly in the order given, so the "REJECT" keyword must come first and "LIMIT" must follow immediately. That ordering is how REJECT is enforced to appear before LIMIT. Once LIMIT has matched, the `OneOf` (the alternative-choice grammar) matches exactly one of two alternatives: a numeric literal, such as `REJECT LIMIT 10` in the test fixture, or the keyword UNLIMITED. The trailing ERRORS keyword is optional. When the segment's `.match()` is called, it uses this `match_grammar` to decide whether the clause matches.

`_Empty` is a direct subclass of `_Sentinel`, both defined in sphinx/sphinx/ext/autodoc/_sentinels.py. `class _Empty(_Sentinel)` is at line 52. Its docstring says it is "a special value for :exclude-members: that never matches to any member".

`_Sentinel` (line 8) is the base class that creates a unique sentinel object. It supplies:
- **Immutability:** it uses `__slots__ = ('_name',)`. `__new__` sets `_name` through `object.__setattr__`. `__setattr__` raises `AttributeError("<name> is immutable")`.
- **Type union support:** `__or__` and `__ror__` return `typing.Union[self, other]` and `typing.Union[other, self]`, so the sentinel can be written as `X | sentinel` in type expressions.
- **Other methods:** `__repr__` returns the name. `__getstate__` raises `TypeError`, so sentinels cannot be pickled.

`_Empty` inherits all of that and adds only `__contains__`, which always returns `False`. Because of this, `member in EMPTY` is never true, so no member is excluded. The sibling class `_All` (line 42) also subclasses `_Sentinel`, but its `__contains__` always returns `True` and it has a no-op `append`.

For type checking, an enum `_EmptyTC` stands in for `_Empty` under `TYPE_CHECKING` (lines 71-76).

The distinction is in `guess_json_utf(data)` in requests/src/requests/utils.py, and `TestGuessJSONUTF` in requests/tests/test_utils.py tests each of the two paths separately. I read the function and the first part of the test class (through line 422). I did not read the rest of the test file.

**1. BOM-based detection.** This runs first, on `sample = data[:4]`.
- If the sample equals `codecs.BOM_UTF32_LE` or `codecs.BOM_UTF32_BE`, it returns `"utf-32"`.
- If `sample[:3] == codecs.BOM_UTF8`, it returns `"utf-8-sig"`.
- If `sample[:2]` is `BOM_UTF16_LE` or `BOM_UTF16_BE`, it returns `"utf-16"`.
- The BOM is kept in the data, so it returns the generic codecs (`utf-16`, `utf-32`, `utf-8-sig`) rather than the endian-specific ones. Those codecs read the BOM themselves to pick the byte order.
- The UTF-32 check comes before the UTF-16 check. A UTF-32-LE BOM, `FF FE 00 00`, starts with the UTF-16-LE BOM, so the order matters. HISTORY.md:707 records a fix for detecting big-endian UTF-32 with a BOM.

**2. Raw byte-pattern detection, with no BOM.** This is a fallback and relies on JSON starting with two ASCII characters. It counts null bytes in the 4-byte sample, using the module constants `_null`, `_null2` and `_null3`.
- 0 nulls: `"utf-8"`.
- 2 nulls: if `sample[::2] == _null2` (bytes 1 and 3 are null), it returns `"utf-16-be"`. If `sample[1::2] == _null2` (bytes 2 and 4 are null), it returns `"utf-16-le"`.
- 3 nulls: if `sample[:3] == _null3`, it returns `"utf-32-be"`. If `sample[1:] == _null3`, it returns `"utf-32-le"`.
- Anything else returns `None`, so the caller can fall back to other detection (HISTORY.md:1227).

**How the tests cover it.**

Python's `utf-32`, `utf-16` and `utf-8-sig` codecs write a BOM, so those three exercise the BOM path. The endian-specific and plain utf-8 codecs write none, so they exercise the null-pattern path.

The request preparation layer normalizes the many shapes a `files=` argument can take into one uniform set of multipart fields. This happens in `RequestEncodingMixin._encode_files(files, data)` in requests/src/requests/models.py. `PreparedRequest` inherits the mixin, and `PreparedRequest.prepare_body(data, files, json)` (models.py:494) calls it when files are supplied.

How it works:
- It validates its input. It raises `ValueError` if `files` is empty or if `data` is a string.
- It flattens `data` and `files` into key/value lists with `to_key_val_list`, so dicts and lists of tuples are both accepted and order is kept for lists.
- Plain form fields from `data` are expanded when a value is iterable. Each value is turned into `str` unless it is already `bytes`, then UTF-8 encoded. Field names that are `bytes` are decoded.
- Each file entry is normalized into `(filename, content, content_type, headers)`:
  - A tuple or list of length 2, 3 or 4 is unpacked as `(fn, fp)`, `(fn, fp, ft)` or `(fn, fp, ft, fh)`. Here `fh` is the custom headers.
  - A bare file object gets its filename from `guess_filename(v)`, falling back to the field name `k`. `guess_filename` is in utils.py:251. It takes `os.path.basename` of the object's `.name` attribute and ignores pseudo-names such as `<stdin>`.
- The content is normalized too:
  - `str`, `bytes` and `bytearray` are used as-is.
  - Objects with `.read()` are read into memory with `fp.read()`.
  - `None` is skipped.
  - Anything else is used as-is.
- Each entry is wrapped in a urllib3 `RequestField(name, data, filename, headers)`. `rf.make_multipart(content_type=ft)` then sets the Content-Disposition and Content-Type headers.
- The rest of the function (not shown above) builds the body and its content type from these fields. I did not read it, so I can't confirm the details; I expect it to use urllib3's `encode_multipart_formdata`.

So the layer's responsibility is to hide the differences between file inputs (dict or list, 2-, 3- or 4-tuples, file objects, strings or bytes) from the transport layer. It hands the transport a consistent body and Content-Type, and the callers don't have to deal with the differences.

The `Linter` class (`sqlfluff/src/sqlfluff/core/linter/linter.py`) decouples dialect grammar from rule validation by routing both through a `FluffConfig` object. The dialect is a plug-in object and the rules are a separately registered set.

1. **Dialect resolution.** `FluffConfig` (`core/config/fluffconfig.py:160`) turns the `dialect` string into a `Dialect` object with `dialect_selector(dialect)`. It stores that object in the private config key `dialect_obj`.

   - It then reads `self.dialect = self.config.get("dialect_obj")` and `self.templater = self.config.get("templater_obj")`.

2. **Grammar lives in the dialect, not the linter.** Each `dialects/dialect_*.py` file defines `BaseSegment` subclasses and grammars (`Sequence`, `OneOf`, and so on), registered in a `Dialect` object. The lexer and parser only ask the dialect for what they need:
   - The lexer calls `config.get("dialect_obj").get_lexer_matchers()` (parser/lexer.py:742).
   - The parser gets the dialect from the config (parser/parser.py, parser/context.py:128).
   - Lookups go through `dialect.ref(...)` and `get_root_segment()`.
   - The linter passes `dialect=config.get("dialect_obj")` when it builds a parse context (linter.py:489 and 538).

   `BaseSegment` (parser/segments/base.py:144) is the common element that drives lexing, parsing and linting. The parse step turns the dialect-specific grammar into a generic tree of segments.

3. **Rules are independent of dialect.** `Linter.get_rulepack()` (linter.py:100-107) calls `get_ruleset()`, which returns the "standard" `RuleSet`, and registers any `user_rules`. It then calls `RuleSet.get_rulepack(config)` (core/rules/base.py:1078), which does the following:
   - It validates the rule config.
   - It applies the allow and deny lists.
   - It instantiates the rules, producing a `RulePack`.

   Rules such as LT09 work only on the segment tree. They use `RuleContext`, `FunctionalContext` and segment-type predicates like `sp.is_type("select_clause_element")`. They never touch grammar definitions directly.

So the linter parses with whatever dialect the config supplies, then runs the config-selected rule pack over the resulting tree. The `FluffConfig` and its `dialect_obj` are the single hand-off point between the two.

Hierarchy (requests/src/requests/exceptions.py): RequestException(IOError) is the root (line 12). Its __init__ pops `response` and `request` kwargs, stores them as .response/.request, and back-fills request from response.request. HTTPError(RequestException) (line 55) and ConnectionError(RequestException) (line 59) are SIBLINGS, not parent/child. ProxyError and SSLError subclass ConnectionError. Timeout subclasses RequestException directly. ConnectTimeout subclasses both ConnectionError and Timeout. ReadTimeout subclasses Timeout. TooManyRedirects, URLRequired, MissingSchema, InvalidSchema and InvalidURL (the last three also ValueError) subclass RequestException. The module also imports urllib3's HTTPError as BaseHTTPError, which is a separate hierarchy.

Propagation:
- Connection-level failures: in adapters.py, HTTPAdapter.send (lines ~658-694) catches urllib3 and OS errors. ProtocolError/OSError, MaxRetryError, ClosedPoolError map to ConnectionError. Other cases map to ConnectTimeout, RetryError, ProxyError, SSLError, ReadTimeout or InvalidHeader. Each is raised with request=request. urllib3 exceptions never reach the caller, because they are translated into the requests hierarchy.
- HTTP status errors: these only arise when Response.raise_for_status() (models.py ~line 999-1026) runs. For 4xx or 5xx it raises HTTPError(msg, response=self). That means a response was received, so .response is populated. Session.send/request does not raise HTTPError on its own.
- Redirect errors: sessions.py:190 raises TooManyRedirects(..., response=resp).

Role of the hierarchy: `except RequestException` catches everything. `except HTTPError` isolates server/client status errors, where e.response.status_code is available and the error can be inspected, such as retrying a 5xx or handling a 404. `except ConnectionError` (or its subclasses, plus Timeout) isolates transport failures, where there is usually no response and a retry or backoff is appropriate. ConnectTimeout is in both ConnectionError and Timeout, so it is safe to retry. Because HTTPError is not a ConnectionError, handlers for one don't accidentally catch the other. Since RequestException derives from IOError (docs/api.rst:222), it is also caught by `except OSError`/`IOError`.

**How `__init__` works**

1. `response = kwargs.pop("response", None)` removes `response` from the keyword arguments, defaulting to `None`, and stores it as `self.response`.
2. `self.request = kwargs.pop("request", None)` does the same for `request`.

   - `response is not None`
   - `not self.request` (no request was passed explicitly)
   - `hasattr(response, "request")` (the response object exposes a `request` attribute)

Both keyword arguments default to `None`, and `*args` is accepted and not consumed. So existing code that raises `RequestException("message")` with no extra arguments still works. Callers that pass `response=` or `request=` get the new context, and callers that don't are unaffected. In sqlfluff's Vertica dialect (dialect_vertica.py), TimeseriesClauseSegment (type "timeseries_clause_statement") is a Sequence of TIMESERIES, an AliasExpressionSegment, AS, a QuotedLiteralSegment and an OverClauseSegment, wrapped in Indent/Dedent. The Vertica UnorderedSelectStatementSegment subclasses the ANSI one and re-declares its match_grammar. That grammar is SelectClause, optional From, Where, GroupBy, Having, Overlaps and NamedWindow. It uses parse_mode GREEDY_ONCE_STARTED. Its terminators are SetOperatorSegment, WithNoSchemaBindingClauseSegment, WithDataClauseSegment, OrderByClauseSegment, LimitClauseSegment and TimeseriesClauseSegment. TimeseriesClauseSegment is therefore a terminator there, so the unordered select stops before a TIMESERIES clause.

Vertica's SelectStatementSegment (extending ansi.SelectStatementSegment) builds its grammar with UnorderedSelectStatementSegment.match_grammar.copy(insert=[...]). The inserted optional elements are OrderByClauseSegment, FetchClauseSegment, LimitClauseSegment, TimeseriesClauseSegment and NamedWindowSegment. The copy would otherwise inherit the unordered select's terminators, including OrderBy, Limit and Timeseries. Those would stop parsing before the newly inserted clauses could match.

To resolve the conflict, the copy call passes replace_terminators=True with a new terminators list of only SetOperatorSegment, WithNoSchemaBindingClauseSegment and WithDataClauseSegment. This replaces the inherited terminators instead of appending to them. The ORDER BY, LIMIT and TIMESERIES terminators are removed, so those clauses parse as part of the full SELECT statement. The unordered variant still treats them as terminators.

**Where the calls are**

It then builds the merged jar with `merge_cookies(merge_cookies(RequestsCookieJar(), self.cookies), cookies)`. The inner call copies the session jar into a fresh `RequestsCookieJar`. The outer call adds the request cookies on top. The result is passed as `cookies=merged_cookies` to `PreparedRequest.prepare` at line 495.
- `Session.resolve_redirects` in `sessions.py:240-242` is the second place. After `extract_cookies_to_jar` pulls in cookies from the redirect response, `merge_cookies(prepared_request._cookies, self.cookies)` adds the session cookies back. `prepare_cookies` is then called to rebuild the Cookie header.

**What `merge_cookies` does** (`requests/src/requests/cookies.py:542-561`)
- It raises `ValueError` if the target is not a CookieJar.
- If the source is a dict, it calls `cookiejar_from_dict(..., overwrite=False)`, so existing cookies are not overwritten.
- If the source is a CookieJar, it calls `cookiejar.update()`. If that raises `AttributeError`, it falls back to `set_cookie` for each cookie.

**How the merged jar is used**
`PreparedRequest.prepare_cookies` (`models.py:610-628`) stores the jar in `self._cookies`. It then builds the `Cookie` header with `get_cookie_header` and sets `self.headers["Cookie"]`. That header is the only way cookies reach the server.

**Impact of removing the calls**
1. **Removing the calls in `prepare_request`:** you would have to pass either `self.cookies` or the request cookies to `prepare`, not both. Passing only the request cookies drops the session's pre-configured cookies, such as a login or session-id cookie, so authenticated requests would fail with 401/403 or a redirect to a login page. Passing only the session cookies ignores the per-request cookies. Either way the Cookie header would be missing half the data.
2. **Isolation would be lost:** the fresh `RequestsCookieJar()` is what keeps per-request cookies out of the session. HISTORY.md:1268 notes that cookies set on individual requests are no longer persisted to the `Session`. Without the copy, the request cookies would be merged into, or replace, `self.cookies`, so they would leak into later requests. Alternatively, `p.prepare` might receive a plain dict or jar and no merged jar at all.
3. **Redirects:** removing the call at `sessions.py:241` means a redirect would send only the cookies from the redirect response and the original request. The session cookies would be lost, and authentication could break part-way through a redirect chain.
4. **Header-based auth is unaffected:** `auth=merge_setting(auth, self.auth)` and the Authorization header do not depend on `merge_cookies`. Only cookie-based authentication would be hurt.

There is no explicit error handling in the REPLACE clause segment. It has only a `match_grammar` and no custom `parse_grammar`. Failure handling comes from how the generic `Delimited` grammar matches.

**The segments**
- `ReplaceClauseSegment` (type `select_replace_clause`) is defined in `dialect_bigquery.py` at line 1331 and in `dialect_snowflake.py` at line 1976.
- Both use `Sequence("REPLACE", Bracketed(Delimited(Sequence(<expr>, "AS", Ref("SingleIdentifierGrammar")))))`.
- BigQuery's expression is `Ref("BaseExpressionElementGrammar")`. Snowflake's is `Ref("ExpressionSegment")`.

**What happens on a malformed pair** (`Delimited.match` in `core/parser/grammar/delimited.py`, about lines 90-191)
- `Delimited` alternates between looking for content and looking for a delimiter. The delimiter defaults to `CommaSegment`. The content is one `expression AS identifier` Sequence.
- Before each step it checks for terminators. If one matches, the loop stops.
- It then calls `longest_match` on the content matchers, or on the delimiter if one is expected. While seeking content, the delimiter is pushed as a terminator so expressions stop at commas.
- If an element fails to match, either because the expression breaks the expression grammar or the alias isn't a valid identifier, then `if not match:` runs. Since `optional_delimiter` is False for `Delimited`, the code hits `break`. No exception is raised.
- The loop ends and returns whatever was matched so far, which is `working_match`. If nothing matched, that is an empty match. It also returns `MatchResult.empty_at(idx)` if `min_delimiters` isn't met. `min_delimiters` defaults to 0, so this doesn't apply to the REPLACE clause.
- A trailing delimiter is only kept if `allow_trailing` is set. The default is False.

**Consequences**
- `Bracketed` expects its closing bracket right after the partial `Delimited` match. If a malformed pair leaves unmatched content before the `)`, the bracket match fails.
- The enclosing `Sequence` then fails, so `ReplaceClauseSegment` doesn't match. The select clause modifier or select target parsing then can't consume the clause.
- The leftover tokens end up in an `UnparsableSegment`, which is reported as a parse error. The failure is therefore a non-match that propagates up, not a raised error.

For each member the rules are applied in this order:

1. **Docstring and privacy info.** It fetches the docstring with `getdoc`. It ignores a docstring that is not a string, and one that merely equals the member's class docstring. It then splits off metadata with `separate_metadata`. `has_doc` is true if a docstring remains. A member is private if the metadata says `:meta private:`. It is public if the metadata says `:meta public:`. Otherwise it is private when its name starts with `_`. A member is treated as an attribute (`isattr`) if it is `INSTANCE_ATTR` or has a doc-comment found by `analyzer.find_attr_docs()`.
2. **Mocked members.** Mocked objects (`ismock`) are skipped unless they have attribute docs.
3. **`:exclude-members:`.** If `membername` is in `self.options.exclude_members`, `keep = False`. That option is parsed by `exclude_members_option` in `_directive_options.py` (line 119) into a set of names. With no argument it becomes the `EMPTY` sentinel, which never matches any member (see `_sentinels.py`).
4. **Special `__methods__`.** When `want_all` is true and the name matches `special_member_re`, the member is kept only if it is listed in the `special-members` option. It must also not be `__doc__`, must not be a filtered inherited member, and must have a docstring or `undoc_members` set.
5. **Documented attributes.** A member with a doc-comment is kept. If it is private and `want_all` is true, it is kept only if it is listed in `private_members`.
6. **Private members.** If `want_all` is true and the member is private, it needs a docstring or `undoc_members`. It must also be listed in `private_members` and not be a filtered inherited member.
7. **Everything else.** It is dropped if `:members:` is `ALL` and `is_filtered_inherited_member` is true. That inner helper walks the class `__mro__` and checks the base classes named in `:inherited-members:`. Otherwise it is kept only if `has_doc or undoc_members`.
8. **Forced skips.** Members with `ObjectMember.skipped` set, such as module attributes not in `__all__`, get `keep = False`.
9. **User override.** Finally it emits the `autodoc-skip-member` event with `emit_firstresult(..., objtype, membername, member, not keep, options)`. Napoleon connects its `_skip_member` to this event to include private, special or `__init__` members, and autosummary emits the same event.
10. **Errors.** If any exception is raised while deciding, the member is dropped and autodoc logs a warning.

Requests does not put version validation in the exception hierarchy. The exceptions only supply a warning type, and the validation lives in requests/__init__.py. Nothing raises to the user, so existing code keeps working.

**Exception side (requests/src/requests/exceptions.py)**
- `RequestsWarning(Warning)` is the base warning class.
- `RequestsDependencyWarning(RequestsWarning)` has the docstring "An imported dependency doesn't match the expected version range." It subclasses `Warning`, not `RequestException`, so a mismatch is reported as a warning and not as a failure. Users can filter it with `warnings.filterwarnings`.
- `FileModeWarning` sits next to it in the same warning branch.

**Validation side (requests/src/requests/__init__.py)**
- `check_compatibility(urllib3_version, chardet_version, charset_normalizer_version)` does the checks.
  - It splits the urllib3 version string, rejects `["dev"]` with an assert, and pads a two-part version such as "16.1" with "0".
  - It then asserts urllib3 >= 1.21.1.
  - If chardet is installed, it asserts `(3,0,2) <= version < (6,0,0)`.
  - Otherwise, if charset_normalizer is installed, it asserts `(2,0,0) <= version < (4,0,0)`.
  - If neither is installed, it calls `warnings.warn(..., RequestsDependencyWarning)`.
- `_check_cryptography(cryptography_version)` returns quietly if the version string can't be parsed (`ValueError`). If the version is below 1.3.4, it emits a `RequestsDependencyWarning` about slowdown.
- Import-time guard:
  - The module wraps the call to `check_compatibility(urllib3.__version__, chardet_version, charset_normalizer_version)` in `try/except (AssertionError, ValueError)`.
  - On failure it calls `warnings.warn("urllib3 (...) or chardet (...)/charset_normalizer (...) doesn't match a supported version!", RequestsDependencyWarning)`.
- Optional imports: `chardet` and `charset_normalizer` are imported inside `try/except ImportError` and set to `None` if missing, so a missing package doesn't break the import.

**Backward-compatibility approach**
- Parse versions defensively.
- Turn assertion and parse failures into a warning that subclasses `Warning`, not an exception.
- Treat optional dependencies as optional.
- Keep the new warning classes inside the existing hierarchy so existing `except RequestException` handlers are unaffected.

`Response.links` (a property on the `Response` class in requests/src/requests/models.py) reads the single `link` header with `self.headers.get("link")`. If the header is present, it calls `parse_header_links(header)` from requests/utils.py. That function strips quotes and spaces from the value and splits it on `", *<"`. For each piece it builds a dict like `{"url": ..., "rel": ..., other params...}`, and it returns the list of these dicts in header order.

`links` then loops over that list with `key = link.get("rel") or link.get("url")` and `resolved_links[key] = link`. The key is the `rel` value, and it falls back to the url when there is no `rel`.

Using `rel` as the dictionary key has three consequences:
- Entries with the same `rel` do not accumulate. Each later entry overwrites the earlier one, so the last entry for a given `rel` wins and the earlier ones are silently dropped. For example, two `rel="next"` links leave only the second.
- Lookup by `rel` is O(1), for example `r.links["next"]`. Building the dict is O(n) over the entries.
- Entries without a `rel` are keyed by their URL. Those can only collide with each other if they share a URL.

To keep every link for a repeated `rel`, you would call `parse_header_links` directly on the header, since it returns the full list.

- `exec_module` runs the module's top-level code with full interpreter privileges. This is arbitrary code execution, and it happens as soon as the config is read. It is not inside Jinja's SandboxedEnvironment.
- Nested modules (names containing `.`) are attached to their parent through `getattr` and `setattr`. The result is returned as a dict with `__`-prefixed names removed.

**Problems**
- Whatever is at the configured path is executed. This includes a path set in a `.sqlfluff` file inside a repository being linted, or a path that is relative or traversal-based (`..`).
- Modules are written into the global `sys.modules` under bare names. They can shadow or poison real modules such as `os` or `json`.
- `walk_packages` imports every module and package found, including unrelated siblings. The code only filters by name prefix (`startswith`), which is a weak check.
- The loaded modules are exposed to templates as plain Python objects. Their functions and attributes can be reached from templates.

**Suggested redesign**
1. Make loading opt-in and disabled by default. Require an explicit trust setting, such as a CLI flag or an environment variable. Do not allow it from repo-local config files, only from trusted user or global config. This matches the guidance in docs/source/production/security.rst.
2. Validate the path. Resolve it with `realpath`. Require it to sit inside the project root or an allow-list of directories. Reject `..` and symlink escapes. Check for `__init__.py` explicitly, and match the module name exactly instead of by prefix.
3. Load only an explicit allow-list of named modules, instead of walking everything under the path.
4. Don't pollute `sys.modules`. Use unique namespaced names, and remove the entries after loading or restore the previous state.
5. Run user module code in a restricted way. Options include a subprocess or a separate process with limited privileges, or a restricted loader. Alternatively, expose only an explicit set of whitelisted callables to the sandboxed Jinja environment. Wrap import errors and exceptions in `SQLFluffUserError`, and log what was loaded.
6. Keep the return shape of the `Libraries` dict, and add tests. The existing fixture `test/fixtures/templater/jinja_m_libraries_module/other/__init__.py` ("Module that should not be loaded") already covers the sibling-module case.

The cookie handling is in `SessionRedirectMixin.resolve_redirects` in requests/src/requests/sessions.py. Each redirect hop runs the same three cookie steps, in this order:

1. **Copy the request.** `prepared_request = req.copy()` at the top of the loop. `PreparedRequest.copy()` also copies the request's `_cookies` jar (via `_copy_cookie_jar` in cookies.py), so changes made on one hop don't mutate the previous request's jar.

2. **Clear the stale header.** `headers.pop("Cookie", None)` removes the `Cookie` header inherited from the previous request. The header is rebuilt from the jar later, so old cookies can't leak onto the new hop.

3. **Extract.** `extract_cookies_to_jar(prepared_request._cookies, req, resp.raw)` pulls the `Set-Cookie` headers from the redirect response into the copied request's jar. It is passed the old `req` because `prepared_request` has already been mutated (new URL, headers popped). The cookie policy therefore matches against the original request.

4. **Merge.** `merge_cookies(prepared_request._cookies, self.cookies)` adds the session's cookie jar to the request jar. This is the `merge_cookies` function in cookies.py, which also works when the jar is a plain `cookielib.CookieJar`. The test `test_cookielib_cookiejar_on_redirect` covers that case.

5. **Prepare.** `prepared_request.prepare_cookies(prepared_request._cookies)` regenerates the `Cookie` header from the merged jar. It does this for the new URL, so only cookies that apply to that URL are sent.

6. **Update the session jar.** After `self.send(..., allow_redirects=False)`, `extract_cookies_to_jar(self.cookies, prepared_request, resp.raw)` stores the new response's cookies in the session jar. The next hop's merge step then picks them up. This keeps `self.cookies` and the per-request jars consistent over many hops.

Other parts of the loop:
- `get_redirect_target(resp)` finds the next URL and ends the loop when there is none.
- `resp.history` is built up as the loop runs.
- When `yield_requests` is true, the prepared request is yielded instead of being sent. In that case step 6 never runs.

On the first request, `Session.prepare_request` (around sessions.py:473) builds `merged_cookies = merge_cookies(merge_cookies(RequestsCookieJar(), self.cookies), cookies)`. That is the starting jar that the redirect loop then copies on each hop.

`SessionRedirectMixin.resolve_redirects` in requests/src/requests/sessions.py is a generator. It handles the three concerns in one loop, in this order.

**Setup.** It keeps a local `hist = []` list. It gets the first redirect target from `get_redirect_target(resp)` and remembers the original URL's fragment.

**Each iteration:**

1. **History.** It copies the last request with `req.copy()`. It appends the current `resp` to `hist` and sets `resp.history = hist[1:]`, so the original response is left out of its own history. The list is rebuilt this way on every pass.

2. **Consuming the body so the socket is released.**
   - It reads `resp.content`.
   - If that raises `ChunkedEncodingError`, `ContentDecodingError` or `RuntimeError`, it falls back to `resp.raw.read(decode_content=False)`.
   - It then checks `len(resp.history) >= self.max_redirects` and raises `TooManyRedirects` if so.
   - Finally it calls `resp.close()`, which returns the connection to the pool.

3. **Building the next request.**
   - It resolves the new URL. A scheme-relative `//` URL gets the scheme added. The previous fragment is re-attached if the new URL has none. Relative locations are joined with `urljoin` and the URL is passed through `requote_uri`.
   - It calls `rebuild_method`.
   - For any status other than 307 or 308, it removes the `Content-Length`, `Content-Type` and `Transfer-Encoding` headers and sets `body = None`. Only 307 and 308 keep the body.
   - It drops the `Cookie` header, then extracts cookies from the response and merges them with the session cookies. It calls `prepare_cookies` to rebuild the header.
   - It calls `rebuild_proxies` and `rebuild_auth`.

4. **Conditionally rewinding the body.**
   - `rewindable = prepared_request._body_position is not None and ("Content-Length" in headers or "Transfer-Encoding" in headers)`.
   - A body that was purged (non-307/308) no longer has those headers, so it is not rewound.
   - A 307/308 request with a file-like or streamed body that has a recorded position is rewound with `rewind_body(prepared_request)`.
   - If `tell()` failed earlier, `_body_position` is a sentinel `object()`. That keeps `rewindable` True, so `rewind_body` raises `UnrewindableBodyError` instead of letting the connection hang.

5. **Sending or yielding.**
   - `req = prepared_request`.
   - If `yield_requests` is set, it yields the request.
   - Otherwise it calls `self.send(req, stream=stream, timeout=..., verify=..., cert=..., proxies=..., allow_redirects=False, **adapter_kwargs)`. It extracts cookies into the session jar, gets the next redirect target and yields the response.

The caller in `Session.send` runs `history = [resp for resp in gen]`.

All three methods live in `SessionRedirectMixin` (requests/src/requests/sessions.py). `Session` inherits from it. `resolve_redirects` is the driver. It calls `get_redirect_target` to decide whether to continue, and it calls `rebuild_auth` on every hop to keep credentials from leaking across hosts.

**`get_redirect_target(resp)`** (line 107)
- If `resp.is_redirect` is true, it reads the `Location` header. It re-encodes the value as latin1 and decodes it as UTF-8 via `to_native_string`, then returns it. Otherwise it returns `None`.
- It does no security checks. It only decides whether there is another hop.

**`resolve_redirects(resp, req, ...)`** (line 159) is a generator.
1. It calls `url = self.get_redirect_target(resp)` (line 175) and loops `while url`.
2. Each iteration copies the previous request with `req.copy()`, appends `resp` to the history, and enforces `max_redirects` by raising `TooManyRedirects`. It consumes and closes the response so the connection returns to the pool.
3. It normalises the URL. It handles `//host` scheme-relative URLs, carries a fragment over from the previous URL, joins relative `Location` values with `urljoin`, and runs `requote_uri`. It then sets `prepared_request.url`.
4. `rebuild_method` switches the method to GET where browsers do (303, 302, and POST after 301). For non-307/308 redirects it strips `Content-Length`, `Content-Type` and `Transfer-Encoding` and clears the body.
5. It always pops the `Cookie` header (lines 234-235). It then rebuilds cookies from the response and the session jar, so cookies are re-evaluated for the new URL.
6. Credential rebuilding happens at lines 245-246. `rebuild_proxies` re-resolves proxies and drops `Proxy-Authorization`. Then `self.rebuild_auth(prepared_request, resp)` runs.
7. It rewinds any rewindable body and sets `req = prepared_request`.
8. It either yields the prepared request (`yield_requests=True`), or sends it with `allow_redirects=False`. In the second case it extracts cookies, calls `url = self.get_redirect_target(resp)` again (line 279) to get the next hop, and yields the response.
9. `Session.send` (around line 720) consumes this generator to build `history`.

**`rebuild_auth(prepared_request, response)`** (line 282) is the security gate.
- It calls `should_strip_auth(response.request.url, prepared_request.url)`. This compares the URL that was just requested with the redirect target.
- If an `Authorization` header is present and `should_strip_auth` returns true, it deletes the header.
- `should_strip_auth` (line 127) returns true if the hostname differs. It returns false for an http→https upgrade on the default ports. It also returns false when the scheme is unchanged and both ports are default. Otherwise it returns true if the port or the scheme changed.
- After stripping, if `trust_env` is set it looks up `.netrc` credentials for the new URL with `get_netrc_auth`. If it finds any, it applies them with `prepare_auth`. The new host therefore gets only its own credentials.

**How they fit together**
- `get_redirect_target` supplies each next URL.
- `resolve_redirects` rebuilds the request for that URL and calls `rebuild_auth` on each hop.
- `rebuild_auth`, through `should_strip_auth`, removes `Authorization` on cross-host or downgrade redirects.
- Cookies and `Proxy-Authorization` are also reset on each hop, so credentials from the original host don't reach a different one.

It then passes the list of `(raw, stack)` tuples to `DepthMap.__init__`. `__init__` builds `self.depth_info[raw.uuid] = DepthInfo.from_raw_and_stack(raw, stack)`. Each `path_to` call is a separate tree search from the root, so nothing is shared between raws. The docstring says this is the less efficient route.

`DepthMap.from_parent(parent)` (depthmap.py:131-138) does `cls(raws_with_stack=parent.raw_segments_with_ancestors)`. `raw_segments_with_ancestors` is a `@cached_property` on BaseSegment (base.py:364-382). It walks `self.segments` once. For each child it builds `PathStep(self, idx, len(self.segments), self._code_indices)`. A raw child is emitted with that single step. A non-raw child recurses into `seg.raw_segments_with_ancestors`, which is cached per segment, and the current step is prepended to each returned stack. The whole tree is therefore traversed once, and the results are reused across calls.

Suggested refactor of `from_raws_and_root`:
1. Reuse the cache. Call `root_segment.raw_segments_with_ancestors` once instead of calling `path_to` per raw. The cached list holds every raw in the root with its full ancestor stack, and sub-segment results are cached as well.
2. Filter to the requested raws. Build `{raw.uuid: stack for raw, stack in root_segment.raw_segments_with_ancestors}` and produce `[(raw, lookup[raw.uuid]) for raw in raw_segments]`, then call `cls(raws_with_stack=...)`. This keeps the order and subset of the input. If the raws are exactly the root's raws, it can simply delegate to `from_parent(root_segment)`.
3. Keep a fallback. Raws that are missing from the lookup, such as newly created segments that were not yet in the tree, can fall back to `root_segment.path_to(raw)` so behaviour stays the same.

The result is one cached O(n) traversal plus dictionary lookups, instead of n separate `path_to` searches. This is the call made from `ReflowSequence.from_raw_segments` (sequence.py ~line 189) when no depth_map is passed.

Response (requests/src/requests/models.py) keeps two separate pieces of state: `_content` and `_content_consumed`. `_content` is the materialized body. It starts as the sentinel `False` (meaning "not read yet"), and later holds bytes, or None if there is no raw stream. `_content_consumed` is a bool recording whether the underlying `raw` stream has been drained.

**Lazy materialization**
- The `content` property (line 891) reads the body only when it is first needed. If `_content is False`, it raises RuntimeError when `_content_consumed` is already True. If `status_code == 0` or `raw is None`, it sets `_content = None`. Otherwise it does `b"".join(self.iter_content(CONTENT_CHUNK_SIZE))`. It then sets `_content_consumed = True` and returns `_content`.
- `iter_content` (line 799) has an inner generator `generate()`. It streams from `raw.stream(...)` (urllib3), or from `raw.read()` for a plain file-like object. It translates urllib3 errors into ProtocolError, DecodeError, ConnectionError and SSLError. When it finishes, it sets `_content_consumed = True`.
- After `generate()`, `iter_content` checks the state. If the content was consumed and `_content` is still the bool `False`, it raises `StreamConsumedError`. If `_content` is already cached, it returns `iter_slices(self._content, chunk_size)`, which replays the cached bytes in chunks. Otherwise it returns the live `generate()` stream. With `decode_unicode`, either source is wrapped in `stream_decode_response_unicode`.
- `iter_lines` builds on `iter_content`, so a streamed response can still be read line by line without loading it all into memory.

**Serialization state management**
- `__attrs__` (line 645) lists only the picklable attributes: `_content`, `status_code`, `headers`, `url`, `history`, `encoding`, `reason`, `cookies`, `elapsed` and `request`. The `raw` stream and the `_content_consumed` flag are deliberately left out.
- `__getstate__` (line 711) first forces materialization. If `_content_consumed` is False, it reads `self.content`, which drains the stream into `_content`. It then returns a dict built from `__attrs__`.
- `__setstate__` (line 719) restores those attributes. It then sets `_content_consumed = True` and `raw = None`. A rehydrated response therefore has no stream, and its `iter_content` replays the cached `_content`. It does not raise, because `_content` is bytes rather than `False`.

**Result**
Streaming stays lazy and one-shot for normal use. Pickling is the only operation that forces the stream to be read. After unpickling, the response behaves as an already-consumed, in-memory response.

In `RequestHooksMixin` (requests/src/requests/models.py), `register_hook(event, hook)` first checks that `event` is a key in `self.hooks`, otherwise it raises ValueError. It then handles `hook` in one of two ways. If `hook` is a Callable, it is appended to `self.hooks[event]` as a single item. Otherwise, if `hook` has `__iter__`, each element that is Callable is added individually with `extend(...)`, and non-callables are silently dropped. The iterable itself is never stored; only its callable members are, flattened into the event's list.

`deregister_hook(event, hook)` is not symmetric with this. It calls `self.hooks[event].remove(hook)` and returns True, or False when remove raises ValueError. `list.remove` removes only the first element equal to `hook`.

- **Registered as a single callable:** `deregister_hook` works, because the callable is in the list.
- **Registered as part of an iterable:** passing the same list or tuple to `deregister_hook` fails. The collection was never stored, so `remove` raises ValueError and the method returns False, and nothing is removed. To remove those hooks you have to deregister each callable one at a time.
- **Non-callable items in the iterable:** they were filtered out at registration, so deregistering them also returns False.
- **Duplicates:** the same callable registered twice, whether directly or via an iterable, appears twice in the list. `remove` takes out only one occurrence per call.

`dispatch_hook` in hooks.py, which wraps a single callable in a list and then iterates, handles the same dual shape. `prepare_hooks` and `PreparedRequest.__init__`-style code pass each value through `register_hook`, so the same flattening applies there.

The list comprehension does not make allocation more efficient. It makes it slightly less efficient, because it trades lazy evaluation for eager allocation:

The logic is in `TLSServer.__init__` in requests/tests/testserver/server.py. `TLSServer` is a subclass of the test `Server` thread class. The constructor does four things in a row:

1. It calls `super().__init__` with the handler, host, port, request count and close event.
2. It stores `cert_chain` and `keyfile`. It then builds `ssl.SSLContext(ssl.PROTOCOL_TLS_SERVER)` and calls `load_cert_chain(cert_chain, keyfile=keyfile)`. This is the certificate-loading concern.
3. It stores `mutual_tls` and `cacert`.
4. If `mutual_tls` is true, it sets `ssl_context.verify_mode = ssl.CERT_OPTIONAL` and calls `load_verify_locations(cacert)`. This is the verification-mode concern. The code assumes the client certificate was issued by the same CA as the server certificate.

`_create_socket_and_bind` later calls `self.ssl_context.wrap_socket(sock, server_side=True)`, then binds and listens.

**Suggested refactor.** Make `TLSServer.__init__` only handle server wiring. Move context creation into two small steps, either private methods or a builder:
- `_load_server_cert(ctx)` calls `load_cert_chain`.
- `_configure_client_verification(ctx)` sets `verify_mode` and calls `load_verify_locations`.

A dedicated `SSLContextBuilder` could expose `with_cert_chain(cert, key)`, `with_mutual_tls(cacert, mode=CERT_OPTIONAL)` and `build()`. `TLSServer` would then take a ready-made `ssl_context`, or a builder, and only use it in `_create_socket_and_bind`.

**Architectural implications.**
- **Separation of concerns.** The server no longer knows about the `ssl` configuration details.
- **Testability.** You can build contexts independently. For example, you could test `CERT_REQUIRED` or a separate client CA, which the current "same CA" assumption rules out. You could also inject a context that is deliberately broken.
- **Reuse and flexibility.** The same builder could serve other test servers. Verify mode would be a parameter, not hard-coded to `CERT_OPTIONAL`.
- **Validation in one place.** For example, the builder could check that `cacert` is provided when `mutual_tls` is set. Today `load_verify_locations(None)` would fail with a confusing error.
- **Costs.** There is an extra abstraction for a small test helper. The `TLSServer` constructor signature would change, so callers such as the fixtures in tests/conftest.py would need updating. Attributes like `self.cert_chain`, `self.keyfile`, `self.mutual_tls` and `self.cacert` may be used elsewhere, so they would need to be kept or migrated. The builder must run before the socket is wrapped, and the context must be fully configured before `wrap_socket`.

In `PreparedRequest.prepare()` (requests/src/requests/models.py), the order is: prepare_method, prepare_url, prepare_headers, prepare_cookies, prepare_body, prepare_auth, then prepare_hooks. The order is sequential because each step reads state that the previous steps wrote to `self`. It is not there for performance.

1. `prepare_auth` comes after `prepare_body`. The code comment says "prepare_auth must be last to enable authentication schemes such as OAuth to work on a fully prepared request." The auth callable is called as `auth(self)` (`AuthBase.__call__(r)` in auth.py). It receives the PreparedRequest and may modify it. Signing schemes such as OAuth or HMAC need the final method, URL, headers and body, because they compute a signature or digest over them, or add an Authorization header. If auth ran before the body was prepared, it would sign an incomplete request. Auth may also change Content-Length or the body, so the body has to exist first. `prepare_auth` also takes the URL, so it can pull in .netrc credentials. That is why the auth step overrides the `headers=` Authorization header, as the docs say.

2. `prepare_hooks` comes after `prepare_auth`. The code comment says "This MUST go after prepare_auth. Authenticators could add a hook." An auth handler can call `r.register_hook(...)` on the request, for example HTTPDigestAuth registers a 401 response hook. `prepare_hooks` loops over the user's hooks and calls `register_hook(event, hooks[event])` for each. If the hooks were prepared before auth, the auth-registered hooks and the user hooks would be set up in the wrong order, or the auth hooks would not be set up as expected. Running hooks last lets the auth hooks be added to the request first, and the user's hooks are then added after them.

Because of these data dependencies (body, then auth, then hooks), the steps cannot be reordered or parallelized. Each step mutates the same PreparedRequest, and auth and hooks need to see the finished result of the earlier steps.

1. sphinx/ext/autodoc/preserve_defaults.py: DefaultValue has only __init__(name) and __repr__. update_defvalue() replaces a parameter's real default with DefaultValue(source_text) via param.replace(default=...) on the function's __signature__.
