2. sphinx/util/inspect.py: DefaultValue is "a simple wrapper for default value of the parameters of overload functions". It has __init__(value), __eq__ (self.value == other, so it equals the plain string such as 'None'), __hash__ (hash(self.value)) and __repr__. signature_from_ast() and _define() create it from ast_unparse(defexpr, code) when building a Signature from a parsed overload definition. inspect.Parameter and Signature compare and hash their defaults, and overload signatures are compared with or looked up against other signatures. So the wrapper has to behave like the string it carries. Defining __eq__ also removes the default __hash__, so __hash__ must be defined alongside it.

In short: the autodoc wrapper is only displayed (init + repr); the overload wrapper is part of Signature/Parameter objects that get compared and hashed (eq + hash, plus repr).

The early-exit check is in `BaseSegment.recursive_crawl()` (sqlfluff/src/sqlfluff/core/parser/segments/base.py). After checking whether the segment itself matches (allow_self / is_type), it runs `if not self.descendant_type_set.intersection(seg_type): return None`. That check stops the whole subtree from being traversed when none of the wanted types appear anywhere below it.

`descendant_type_set` (same file, around line 330) is a `@cached_property`. It returns a frozenset built from every child's `descendant_type_set | class_types`, so it covers all types in the subtree and excludes the segment's own types. Each segment computes its set once, by unioning its children's already-cached sets. After that, the check is a cheap set intersection with the small `seg_type` tuple.

Without the check, `recursive_crawl` would descend into every child of every branch, recursing and yielding through generators at each level. It would do this even for branches that can't contain a match. On deeply nested trees with many irrelevant branches, that cost grows with the size of the tree. With the check, each irrelevant branch is rejected at its root in roughly constant time, so the cost follows only the branches that contain matches. The recursive calls on child segments run the same check, so pruning happens at every level.

Related mechanisms:
- `no_recursive_seg_type` skips whole segment types before recursing.
- `RootOnlyCrawler`/`SegmentSeekerCrawler` in core/rules/crawlers.py:105 prunes the same way, using `self.types & context.segment.descendant_type_set`.

In requests/src/requests/structures.py, CaseInsensitiveDict (a MutableMapping) keeps an OrderedDict `_store` that maps `key.lower()` to a `(original_key, value)` tuple. `__setitem__` (line 46-49), `__getitem__` (line 51-52) and `__delitem__` (line 54-55) each call `key.lower()` on every operation.

Why it costs performance: `str.lower()` is O(len(key)). It allocates a new string every time, even when the key is already lowercase, and the result is thrown away after one dict lookup. The new string has no cached hash, so the dict has to hash it again from scratch. The original key's cached hash is never used. With high-frequency lookups, such as the same header names read over and over across many large dicts, this adds up. Each call also goes through a Python-level method, and that includes the indirect calls from MutableMapping helpers like `get`, `__contains__`, `pop`, `update` and `setdefault`. `copy()` and `__eq__` add more cost: `__eq__` builds a new CaseInsensitiveDict from the other mapping, then `dict(lower_items())` for both sides.

Optimization strategies:
- Memoize the normalization. Keep a small cache, e.g. `functools.lru_cache` on a module-level `_lower(key)` function or a dict of `key -> lowered`. Repeated header names then skip the lower() and the rehash.
- Skip lowering for keys that are already lowercase or that were seen before. A fast path could be `self._store.get(key)` first, which works because lowercase keys hit directly.
- Use `str.casefold`, or normalize once at the boundary, for example when headers are parsed. Callers that already hold a lowered key can use `lower_items()` or access `_store` directly.
- Store interned lowercase keys. Interned strings have a cached hash and fast identity comparison.
- Compute the lowered key once per operation, and in bulk operations like `update` or `copy` reuse the already-lowered keys from `_store` rather than lowering again.

ASTParenExpr (defined in both sphinx/domains/cpp/_ast.py and sphinx/domains/c/_ast.py) implements __eq__ so that it returns NotImplemented when `other` is not an ASTParenExpr. NotImplemented is Python's binary-operator protocol sentinel, not an error and not False. It tells the interpreter that this class does not know how to compare with that type, so `==` falls back to the reflected `other.__eq__(self)`. If that also returns NotImplemented, Python falls back to identity comparison, which yields False. Returning False directly would stop the other operand from getting a chance to handle the comparison and would break symmetry with other types. It also keeps the `-> bool` annotation consistent with the standard convention. When `other` is an ASTParenExpr, __eq__ returns `self.expr == other.expr`. __hash__ is defined as hash(self.expr), so equality and hashing stay consistent. The same pattern appears in ASTParenAttribute in util/cfamily.py, which compares id and arg.

`_body_position` records three states that a boolean can't separate. A boolean would lose either the seek offset or the "tell() failed" case.

1. `None` is the initial value, set in `PreparedRequest.__init__` (models.py:344). It means no position was recorded: the body is absent, is a plain string or bytes, or is a stream with no `tell`. Nothing was consumed from a stream, so a redirect can resend the body as is, and no rewind is needed.

2. An integer is the real offset from `body.tell()`, recorded in `prepare_body` (models.py:532-537) before the body is read. This is the offset that `rewind_body` in utils.py:1071 seeks back to. A boolean could only say "rewindable"; it couldn't say where to rewind to. For example, `test_rewind_partially_read_body` expects `_body_position == 4` for a file that was already partly read. The offset has to be kept so that a redirect resends the body from the original starting point, not from byte 0.

3. A bare `object()` sentinel is stored when `tell()` exists but raises `OSError` (models.py:539-541). It is deliberately not `None` and not an integer. In sessions.py:248, `rewindable = prepared_request._body_position is not None and ("Content-Length" in headers or "Transfer-Encoding" in headers)` is therefore True. `rewind_body` runs and finds that `isinstance(_body_position, integer_types)` is False, so it raises `UnrewindableBodyError`. This is better than hanging the connection by resending a half-consumed body that the server expects `Content-Length` bytes of. If the failure were stored as `None`, the code would treat the request as having no body to rewind. If a boolean were used, the failed-tell case would have to be encoded separately, and the offset would need another attribute.

The `object()` sentinel is a unique value that cannot be mistaken for an offset or for "unset". Together with the `is not None` check and the `isinstance(..., integer_types)` check, it lets one attribute carry "not applicable", "rewind to N" and "should be rewindable but can't be".

`OperatorClassReferenceSegment` (Postgres dialect) subclasses `ansi.ObjectReferenceSegment`. It sets `type = "operator_class_reference"` and adds no other code. It gets all its parsing from the ANSI base class, which handles dotted, possibly schema-qualified identifiers. The `type` string gives the node its own name in the parse tree, and that name is what the YAML test fixtures and any rules check.

`IndexElementOptionsSegment` (`type = "index_element_options"`) uses it through `Ref("OperatorClassReferenceSegment", exclude=Sequence("NULLS", OneOf("FIRST","LAST")))`. The `Ref` looks the segment up by class name in the dialect's library. The `exclude` stops the reference from consuming the `NULLS FIRST/LAST` keywords. The grammar is `COLLATE <collation>`, then an optional operator class followed by an optional `RelationOptionsSegment` for the opclass arguments, then `ASC|DESC` and `NULLS FIRST|LAST`.

`IndexElementSegment` (`type = "index_element"`) wraps a column reference, a function or a bracketed expression, followed by an optional `IndexElementOptionsSegment`. CREATE INDEX, `ALTER TABLE ... ADD CONSTRAINT` and the table-constraint forms (UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY, EXCLUDE) all use that element. Operator classes such as `gist_trgm_ops` are therefore parsed and tagged as `operator_class_reference` in those places. The fixtures create_index.yml, create_table.yml and alter_table.yml show those nodes.

A separate `OperationClassReferenceSegment` at about line 5147 is used at line 5223 and follows the same pattern.

The function is `parse(app, text, docname='index')` in sphinx/testing/restructuredtext.py. It is expensive because each call does a full docutils parse and transform pass, and the tests then check the result with `assert_node`, which recurses over the tree.

**What each call does**
- It builds a new `RSTParser` and attaches the app's config and env to it.
- It sets `env.current_document.docname`, then clears it again in a `finally` block.
- It calls `sphinx.util.docutils._parse_str_to_doctree`. That function creates a new document with the settings overrides (`env`, `gettext_compact`, `input_encoding`, and so on). It then runs the parser and applies every transform from `registry.get_transforms()`, which is Sphinx's whole transform set.
- So each call is a complete read → parse → transform cycle on a new document. Nothing is cached or shared between calls.

**What the tests add**
- After `parse`, the domain tests (for example test_domain_rst.py, test_domain_py*.py, test_domain_std.py, test_domain_js.py) call `assert_node`, defined in sphinx/testing/util.py.
- `assert_node` is recursive. For a list `cls` it checks `node[0]` and then recurses into `node[0]` with the rest of the list. For a tuple it checks the child count and recurses into every child. For a string or class it does an equality or `isinstance` check. For keyword arguments it checks attributes.
- Each call therefore walks the nested expected-structure and the doctree, asserting at every level. The walk is linear in tree size.

**Why it scales badly**
- The parse and transform cost is repeated in full for every scenario, with no sharing of setup or results.
- Across hundreds of similar domain scenarios, the per-call overhead (transform pipeline plus recursive assertions) adds up to a large share of the suite's runtime.
- The domain tests that use `parse` also need a `Sphinx` app/env fixture. The tests that parse signatures directly, such as test_domain_c.py and test_domain_cpp.py with their own `parse`/`check` helpers, avoid this cost.

I did not open the individual domain test files. I did not confirm which of them call this `parse` helper.

In `PreparedRequest.prepare_body(self, data, files, json=None)` (requests/src/requests/models.py), `NotImplementedError("Streamed bodies and files are mutually exclusive.")` is raised at line 543. This is a deliberate limitation rather than an oversight. Requests has no code path that can combine a stream with files, so it fails explicitly.

**How the function branches**
- `is_stream` is true when `data` has `__iter__` and is not a str, bytes, list, tuple or Mapping. That covers file objects, generators and iterators.
- In the stream branch, `body = data` is passed through as-is.
  - The length comes from `super_len(data)`, or `None` if that fails.
  - If the object has `tell()`, the position is saved in `self._body_position` so the body can be rewound on a redirect.
  - Then the `if files:` check raises the error.
  - Otherwise the code sets `Content-Length`, or `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` when the length is unknown.
- In the non-stream branch, with `files` set, it calls `self._encode_files(files, data)`. That returns `(body, content_type)` and the Content-Type header is set from it. Without files, the data is form-encoded with `_encode_params`.

**Why the two can't be merged**
- A stream is meant to be sent lazily and unchanged. The body is the stream object itself, and the length is either known up front or sent chunked.
- A multipart body needs the opposite. `_encode_files` (line 137) builds a list of fields, and for each file it does `fdata = fp.read()`. Then it calls `encode_multipart_formdata(new_fields)`, which builds one complete in-memory bytes body with boundaries.
- Merging a stream into that would mean one of two things:
  - Reading the whole stream into memory. That defeats streaming and breaks for infinite or huge generators, and it would invalidate the `_body_position` rewind handling.
  - Writing a new streaming multipart encoder. That would need boundary handling, length computation and per-part headers, and `requests` doesn't implement it.
- Silently choosing one of the two would drop data or change semantics, so requests refuses.
- The `data` argument is also used as form fields in `_encode_files`. It expects a dict or a list of tuples, and it raises `ValueError` if `data` is a string. A stream is not a valid form-field source there.

**Workaround**: use the third-party `requests-toolbelt` `MultipartEncoder`. It streams multipart bodies and can be passed as `data=` with its own Content-Type header.

The warning goes through the formatter's single output path so it is styled and sent to the same place as all other CLI output.

- `dispatch_dialect_warning` is declared abstract on the `FormatterInterface` in `core/formatter.py:47`. This lets the core `Linter` raise a warning without knowing anything about the CLI.
- At `core/linter/linter.py:768-775`, the linter checks whether the linted file has `SQLParseError` violations. If so, and a formatter is present, it calls `formatter.dispatch_dialect_warning(parsed.config.get("dialect"))`. This is the "dialect might be misconfigured" safety check.
- `OutputStreamFormatter.dispatch_dialect_warning` (`cli/formatters.py:216`) is the CLI implementation. It runs `self._dispatch(self.format_dialect_warning(dialect))`.
- `format_dialect_warning` (`cli/formatters.py:596`) builds the message: "WARNING: Parsing errors found and dialect is set to '<dialect>'. Have you configured your dialect correctly?". It wraps the text in `self.colorize(..., Color.light)`, so colour is applied, or left out when output is plain or `nocolor` is set.
- `_dispatch` (`cli/formatters.py:111`) is the routing point, and the code comment says it is designed for subclassing. It drops empty messages when `_filter_empty` is set. Otherwise it writes the string to `self._output_stream`, which can be stdout or a `FileOutput`.

The method integrates with `_dispatch` so the warning is formatted by the formatter and sent to the configured output stream, like every other `dispatch_*` method, for example `dispatch_persist_filename`. Subclasses can also override `_dispatch` once to redirect all output. The code carries `# pragma: no cover`, so this path is not covered by tests.

The verification in `test_compile_all_catalogs` (sphinx/tests/test_intl/test_catalogs.py) calls `app.builder.compile_all_catalogs()`. It then walks the same `LC_MESSAGES` directory twice with `Path.rglob`. The first walk, `catalog_dir.rglob('*.po')`, collects the source files and maps each to `.with_suffix('.mo')` to build the `expect` set. The second walk, `catalog_dir.rglob('*.mo')`, collects the compiled files into the `actual` set. The test then asserts `actual` is non-empty and equals `expect`.

Each `rglob` is a full recursive scan of the tree, so the filesystem is traversed twice: once for `*.po` and once for `*.mo`. Each walk does a directory listing (`scandir`) at every level and matches every entry against the glob pattern. The cost is therefore proportional to the number of directories and files, and it is paid twice. It could be paid once by listing the tree a single time and filtering by suffix. With thousands of locale catalog files, that doubles the filesystem I/O and pattern matching. `rglob` is also lazy, but the test wraps each call in `set(...)`, so it materializes every path in memory. The set comprehension and the set comparison add further per-file work.

`test_compile_update_catalogs` repeats the same two-walk pattern at lines 91-92. `test_compile_specific_catalogs` walks `*.mo` once at line 69 and again at line 73. The product code in `sphinx/util/i18n.py:152` also uses `locale_path.rglob('*.po')` to find catalogs.

I did not time any of this, so the performance impact is inferred from the code rather than measured.

`guess_filename` (requests/src/requests/utils.py, line 251) is a defensive filter on the `name` attribute of a file-like object. It is not a complete security control. `RequestEncodingMixin._encode_files` in models.py calls it at line 185 (`fn = guess_filename(v) or k`) when a `files=` value is a bare file-like object with no explicit filename. The returned value goes into the multipart `Content-Disposition` filename.

How it works (line 254):
- `name = getattr(obj, "name", None)` reads the attribute safely. Objects with no `name` give None, so there is no AttributeError and no made-up filename.
- `isinstance(name, basestring)` rejects non-string names. For example, `open(fd_int)` or a file built from a descriptor has an integer `name`. This was the fix for #2356 ("Fix filename type check for multipart form-data uploads"). It stops the encoder from receiving a non-string and failing, or encoding it wrongly, in the multipart header.
- `name[0] != "<" and name[-1] != ">"` rejects pseudo-names such as `<stdin>`, `<fdopen>` or `<socket>`. These are not real files, and sending them would leak internal or meaningless details as the filename.
- `os.path.basename(name)` strips any directory components. The local path (for example `/home/user/secret/data.txt`) is not disclosed to the server. The path-traversal and path-leak risk in the filename the server sees is removed.
- If any check fails, the function returns None. `_encode_files` then falls back to the form field key `k` as the filename.

Tests: `test_guess_filename_invalid` asserts None for bad values, and `test_guess_filename_valid` checks valid names in test_utils.py.

In `morsel_to_cookie` (requests/src/requests/cookies.py), the function has to give `http.cookiejar.Cookie` an absolute expiry. A `Cookie` stores `expires` as an absolute Unix timestamp in seconds. A `Morsel` can carry two different attributes for this: the relative `max-age` and the absolute `expires` date string. The function starts with `expires = None` and checks `max-age` first (`if morsel["max-age"]:`). This follows RFC 6265, where Max-Age takes precedence over Expires when both are present.

- **max-age branch:** the relative value is converted with `expires = int(time.time() + int(morsel["max-age"]))`. It is the current epoch time (`time.time()`) plus the max-age delta in seconds, truncated to an int. If `int(...)` raises `ValueError` because max-age isn't numeric, the function raises `TypeError(f"max-age: ... must be integer")`.
- **expires branch:** this runs only when there is no max-age (`elif morsel["expires"]:`). The date string is parsed with `time.strptime` using the template "%a, %d-%b-%Y %H:%M:%S GMT". `calendar.timegm` then turns the parsed struct_time into an absolute UTC epoch value. For example, "Thu, 01-Jan-1970 00:00:01 GMT" gives 1.
- **Neither attribute set:** `expires` stays `None`, so the cookie is a session cookie.

The resulting `expires` is passed to `create_cookie(...)` along with the comment, domain, path, name, value, secure, httponly (in `rest`) and version fields.

The tests in requests/tests/test_requests.py cover these cases. They check that `expires` is None, that a date string converts to 1, that max-age=60 gives an int, and that max-age="woops" raises `TypeError`.

The method is `PythonDomain.find_obj` (sphinx/domains/python/__init__.py:865). It reconciles fully-qualified and unqualified references by trying candidate names in a fixed, deterministic priority order, from most specific to least specific. It only falls back to a fuzzy suffix match in the one mode where that is allowed.

How it works:
- It first strips a trailing `()` and returns `[]` if the name is empty.
- It then picks one of two modes with `searchmode`.
- **searchmode 0 (default, exact):** The object type is not considered. It checks candidates in this order, and the first hit wins:
  1. `name` as given, which is the fully-qualified or top-level case.
  2. If `type == 'mod'`, it returns `[]`, because modules only allow exact matches.
  3. `classname.name`.
  4. `modname.name`.
  5. `modname.classname.name`.
  Because the exact name is tried first, a fully-qualified reference is never shadowed by a context-relative one. An unqualified name is resolved relative to the current `py:module` and `py:class` context, which `PyXRefRole.process_link` stores on the pending node. A single deterministic result is returned.
- **searchmode 1 (refspecific, for a leading `.` in the target):**
  1. It builds the list of object types allowed for the role.
  2. It tries `modname.classname.name`, then `modname.name`, then `name`. Each candidate must have a matching objtype.
  3. Only if none of those match does it do "fuzzy" matching: every object whose name ends with `.name` and has an allowed objtype is returned. This can produce several matches, and `resolve_xref` then handles the ambiguity.

The result is a list of `(fullname, ObjectEntry)` tuples. The specific-to-general order keeps resolution predictable while still letting short names work. Ambiguity is only possible in the explicit fuzzy mode.

In requests/src/requests/cookies.py, class MockRequest (the wrapper that makes a requests Request look like a urllib2.Request for http.cookiejar) parses the same, unchanging self._r.url several times. __init__ calls urlparse(self._r.url).scheme to set self.type. get_host() calls urlparse(self._r.url).netloc on every call. get_origin_req_host() and the `host` and `origin_req_host` properties all delegate to get_host(), so they re-parse as well. get_full_url() calls urlparse again, plus urlunparse, whenever a custom Host header is set. http.cookiejar calls these methods many times per request: add_cookie_header and extract_cookies call request_host/request_path/get_full_url for each cookie and domain policy check (return_ok, domain_return_ok, set_ok). A wrapper is created in extract_cookies_to_jar and get_cookie_header for every request and redirect. In high-volume jar operations the same URL is therefore parsed over and over. urlparse does string splitting and validation and, although it has a small internal cache, it still builds a new ParseResult namedtuple each time. The result is wasted CPU and allocations that grow with the number of cookies and requests.

Optimization: parse once and cache. In __init__, do `self._parsed = urlparse(request.url)` (or lazily on first use with functools.cached_property). Then set self.type = self._parsed.scheme, make get_host return self._parsed.netloc, and have get_full_url reuse self._parsed (cache the rebuilt URL too, when the Host header override is present). The request is treated as read-only: the wrapper only reads url and headers and never mutates them. All new headers still go into the separate self._new_headers dict through add_unredirected_header. The cached values are therefore safe, because the wrapped request's URL does not change during the wrapper's short lifetime. Callers can also build the wrapper once and reuse it rather than re-wrapping.

The exception is a plain marker class, `UnsupportedMultiCharacterCharLiteral(Exception)` in sphinx/util/cfamily.py:287. The AST node constructor raises it, and the parser catches it and turns it into a parser error.

1. **Where it is raised.** `ASTCharLiteral.__init__(prefix, data)` is in sphinx/domains/c/_ast.py:281-289, and the C++ version is in sphinx/domains/cpp/_ast.py:~501. It decodes the literal body with `data.encode().decode('unicode-escape')`. If the decoded string has length 1, it stores `self.value = ord(decoded)`, which is the valid single-character case. Otherwise it raises `UnsupportedMultiCharacterCharLiteral(decoded)`, which is the multi-character case, for example `'ab'`. Because the check sits in the constructor, no AST node is created for an invalid literal.

2. **Where it is caught.** `_parse_literal` in sphinx/domains/c/_parser.py (~lines 151-165) and in sphinx/domains/cpp/_parser.py (~lines 220-233) does this:
   - It matches `char_literal_re` and takes the prefix from group 1 and the data from group 2.
   - It then calls `ASTCharLiteral(prefix, data)` inside a `try` block.
   - `except UnicodeDecodeError as e` calls `self.fail('Can not handle character literal. Internal error was: %s' % e)`.
   - `except UnsupportedMultiCharacterCharLiteral` calls `self.fail('Can not handle character literal resulting in multiple decoded characters.')`.

3. **How `fail` ties it into error handling.** `self.fail` is the `BaseParser` method in sphinx/util/cfamily.py. It raises a `DefinitionError`, which the surrounding parse code and the callers of `_parse_literal` treat as an ordinary parse failure. The C++ parser also collects these errors, for example through `_make_multi_error`, and tries alternative parses. A valid single-character literal returns the AST node (the C++ parser wraps it with `_udl(char_lit)`). A multi-character literal becomes a clear `DefinitionError` at the right position instead of an uncaught generic exception.

BaseAdapter (requests/src/requests/adapters.py) is a root only within the adapter hierarchy; in Python every class implicitly inherits from `object`, so `super().__init__()` there just calls `object.__init__()`, which does nothing. The call is a deliberate cooperative-inheritance (MRO-friendly) choice. It keeps the initializer chain intact if BaseAdapter is mixed with other classes in a multiple-inheritance hierarchy. For example, a user-defined adapter such as `class MyAdapter(BaseAdapter, SomeMixin)` would have its mixin's `__init__` reached through BaseAdapter. It also means that if a parent class is added later, initialization will still propagate without editing BaseAdapter. BaseAdapter is an abstract interface/template: `send()` and `close()` raise NotImplementedError, and subclasses such as HTTPAdapter (which extends BaseAdapter, and which Session.get_adapter returns from the mounted adapters) override them. So the pattern is a cooperative `super()` call, Python's cooperative multiple inheritance, which keeps the abstract base class open to extension. The call has no effect today.

I did not find any place where `StructTypeSegment` is instantiated repeatedly, so this answer comes from reading how the grammar is wired. I did not measure allocation or GC. The "segment class that parses structured data type definitions" is `StructTypeSegment`. The base class is in `dialect_ansi.py:901` (`type = "struct_type"`, `match_grammar = Nothing()`). Dialect subclasses are in `dialect_hive.py:281`, `dialect_sparksql.py:1168`, `dialect_bigquery.py:1368`, `dialect_duckdb.py:198` and `dialect_athena.py:355`. Each subclass defines `match_grammar = Sequence("STRUCT", Ref("StructTypeSchemaSegment", optional=True))`.

`StructTypeSchemaSegment` is the bracketed `<name: type, ...>` part. It contains `Ref("DatatypeSegment")`, which can lead back to `StructTypeSegment`. That is how deeply nested `STRUCT<a: STRUCT<b: STRUCT<...>>>` definitions are parsed.

**Why reusing the shared grammar object is cheaper**
- The grammar is declared once, as the class-level `match_grammar`. It is built when the dialect is defined and expanded.
- Nested types are written as `Ref("StructTypeSegment")` and `Ref("StructTypeSchemaSegment")`. A `Ref` is a small name-only, late-bound reference (`core/parser/grammar/base.py:322`).
- At match time, `Ref.match` calls `_get_elem(dialect)` (`base.py:372`, `:407`). That calls `Dialect.ref(name)` (`core/dialects/base.py:285`), which returns the already-built object from `dialect._library`.
- So every nesting level reuses the same single `StructTypeSegment` class and grammar tree. The only per-level work is the match itself, plus the segment node that is created when a match succeeds.
- `Ref.simple` is wrapped in `@cached_method_for_parse_context`, so the lookup and hint work is cached per parse context.

**Why creating a new segment or grammar at each level costs more**
- The segment class carries a whole `match_grammar` tree of `Sequence`, `Bracketed`, `Delimited` and `Ref` objects. A fresh instance at each nesting level would rebuild or copy that tree every time.
- That would allocate many short-lived objects at every depth. The cost grows with nesting depth and with backtracking through `OneOf` branches.
- Those objects would be thrown away after each attempt. That adds GC pressure.
- Fresh instances would also lose the parse-context caches on the shared objects (`cached_method_for_parse_context`, as used for `Ref.simple`). The parser would then redo work it would otherwise have cached.
- The `Ref`-based design avoids this by letting the one shared definition be looked up by name. This keeps memory flat and recursion cheap.
